newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peron's widow denies "dirty war" repression.
newsitem.headline: Peron's widow denies "dirty war" repression.

text.p: The widow of former Argentine President Juan Domingo Peron denied on Monday any role in the repression of leftist rebels during Argentina's "dirty war".
Maria Estela Martinez de Peron, nicknamed "Isabelita", appeared in Spain's High Court to testify about the disappearance of some 300 Spaniards under a military dictatorship from 1976-1983.
Isabelita married Peron after the death of his wife Evita and was his vice president. After Peron's death, she took over as President in 1974 until a military coup in March 1976.
Lawyers for the missing Spaniards argued that the repression of leftist militants under military juntas that ruled Argentina from 1976-1983 actually began earlier under Isabelita Peron.
Lawyers told reporters after the testimony that Peron claimed to be the victim of conspiracy and could not remember certain facts when questioned.
"She considers herself a puppet, somebody who didn't have any decisive influence nor knowledge of the events that took place when she was president," lawyer Angel Garcia Castillejo said.
Peron, who now lives in Spain, was summoned to the court by leading Spanish judge Baltazar Garzon. Garzon has called more than 100 officers of the 1976-1983 military regime.

"I am used to obeying the laws and being at least cordial with the country that provides me with refuge," Peron told reporters after testifying for more than five hours. "If the Spanish judiciary needs me, my moral obligation is to come."
Outside the courtroom, about 20 family members of missing Spaniards cursed Peron and pelted her with eggs as she left.

Garzon has also summoned the man who toppled Isabelita Peron, former military president Jorge Videla, and ex-navy officer Adolfo Scilingo who confessed in 1995 to "death flights" in which thousands of suspected leftists were detained, tortured and then thrown to their deaths over the River Plate.
Officially, 14,000 people died or "disappeared" in the dirty war, most of them probably kidnapped, tortured and killed by the security forces.
Former junta members were tried in 1985 but Peronist President Carlos Menem pardoned them all after he came to power in 1989.
Rights groups hope a Spanish trial will end in international arrest warrants which could prevent dirty war criminals from traveling abroad.

Ex-Navy Capt. Alfredo Astiz, the "Blond Angel" and a member of the anti-guerilla squad that operated out of the infamous Navy School of Mechanics in Buenos Aires, was tried in absentia in France and given a life sentence for killing two French nuns. He is also wanted by Sweden for killing a Swedish student.
